subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: What Are We Measuring and With What?

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the picture; put a tick mark if length, height, weight, depth, breadth, or temperature is being measured.
What is being used to measure height? What other tools can be used?
Recall Grade 3 learning; check and fill blanks — are the given classroom length statements correct or incorrect?

time_bands.activity: Open with the classroom scene. Pairs look at the picture in Let Us Observe Q1 (p.80) ("put a tick mark if length, height, weight…") and discuss which attributes are being measured before sharing with the class.

Class discusses Let Us Observe Q2 (p.80) ("what is being used to measure height?…"). Students name the tool in the picture, then suggest other tools they have seen used to measure height, listing them on the board.

Students work individually on Let Us Observe Q3 (p.80) ("check and fill blanks — are the given classroom length statements correct or incorrect?"). They draw on their body-scale sense of a metre to judge each statement, then pairs compare answers and resolve disagreements.
Brief whole-class share: which statements were correct and why? Teacher surfaces any mismatch between students' intuitions and the metre benchmark to sharpen the class's sense of relative size.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often confuse the attribute being measured (length, depth, breadth) with the tool used; the picture discussion in Q1 is designed to separate these ideas. A common slip in Q3 is judging a student's height as more than a metre when it may not be — encourage students to mime the metre length with their arms before deciding. No measurement tools are needed for this unit; the work is entirely observational and recall-based.

periods.activity_title: Walk, Jump, Crawl — Feeling Metric Distances

tasks_in_class.description: Draw 1 m, 5 m, and 10 m lines on the floor; walk, jump, and crawl on the lines.
Long jump competition: estimate then measure each student's jump distance using rope combinations; fill the table.

homework.description: Estimate how long and broad the classroom is; measure and check.

time_bands.activity: Students cut or measure metre, half-metre, and quarter-metre lengths of rope. They then carry out Let Us Do Q1 (p.81) ("draw 1 m, 5 m, and 10 m lines on the floor; walk, jump, and crawl on the lines") in the classroom or corridor, moving along each line in turn.

Long-jump activity from Let Us Do Q2 (p.82) ("long jump competition: estimate then measure each student's jump distance…"). Each child first estimates their jump distance in metres and fractions, then jumps; a partner measures using rope combinations. Results go into the table in the book.

Whole-class debrief: students share whose estimate was closest and which rope combination they used most. Teacher asks: 'What did you use when the jump was between two rope lengths?' to surface the idea of combining rope pieces.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently over-estimate their jump distance before measuring; the gap between estimate and actual is productive — invite them to explain why their estimate was off rather than correcting silently. For homework, students estimate and then measure the length and breadth of the classroom using their rope, recording both in the table from Let Us Do Q3 (p.82); a family member can hold one end of the rope. Rope pieces of 1 m, ½ m, and ¼ m are needed; these can be string, wool, or cut strips.
materials: String or wool cut into 1 m, half-metre, and quarter-metre lengths
Chalk or tape to mark floor lines

section_titles: Estimating Lengths of Animals and Objects
periods.activity_title: From Whales to Erasers — Two Scales of Length

tasks_in_class.description: Answer 5 questions: bus length, bats per whale, buses per two whales, stacked ostriches, crocodiles per whale — using pictured reference lengths.
Compare the metre rope with a tailor's measuring tape; observe the marks and discuss how they help measure clearly.
Observe the 1 cm red bar repeated 10 times to make 10 cm; fill: 1/2 m = ___ cm, 1/4 m = ___ cm.

time_bands.activity: Students open to p.83 and study the animal pictures. They work in pairs on Let Us Think Q1–Q5 (p.83) ("answer 5 questions: bus length, bats per whale, buses per two whales…"), using the given reference lengths as multipliers or divisors to reason through each comparison.

Teacher holds up a metre rope alongside a tailor's measuring tape for Let Us Observe (p.84) ("compare the metre rope with a tailor's measuring tape; observe the marks…"). Students describe what they notice about the markings and discuss why smaller marks are useful for objects like an eraser.

Students work on Let Us Observe (red bar) (p.84) ("observe the 1 cm red bar repeated 10 times; fill 1/2 m = ___ cm, 1/4 m = ___ cm"). They count the red bars to confirm that 10 cm make up the strip, then use the relationship 1 m = 100 cm to fill the blanks.

periods.teacher_notes: In the animal-lengths task, students often add reference lengths correctly but stumble when division is needed (e.g. how many 6 m crocodiles fit in a 30 m whale); encourage drawing repeated jumps of the crocodile length along the whale as a pictorial strategy. When the tape is introduced, a common confusion is thinking the tape's centimetre marks are a different unit from the metre — explicitly lay the rope alongside the tape and count 100 marks together. The relationship 1 m = 100 cm established here is the key symbolic fact students carry into all subsequent measuring work.

periods.activity_title: Measure, Rank, and Race — Working with the Centimetre Scale

tasks_in_class.description: Measure each drawn object using a scale; write the names in increasing order of length.
Estimate lengths (fingernail, eraser, ant, grain, rajma): equal to, more than, or less than 1 cm; verify by measuring. Write things shorter than 1 cm.
Race three toy cars down a ramp; measure the distance each travels in cm and rank them.

time_bands.activity: Each student uses a ruler to carry out Let Us Do Q1 (p.85) ("measure each drawn object using a scale; write the names in increasing order of length"). Teacher reminds the class to align the zero mark of the scale with one end of the object before reading.

Students work on Let Us Do Q2 (p.86) ("estimate lengths — fingernail, eraser, ant, grain, rajma — equal to, more than, or less than 1 cm; verify by measuring"). They first fill the estimate column, then measure each item and fill the actual column, noting items shorter than 1 cm.

Groups of three set up a simple ramp using a book and a ruler and carry out Let Us Do Q3 (p.86) ("race three toy cars down a ramp; measure the distance each travels in cm and rank them"). Each group records distances and decides the winner by measurement, not by eye.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in Q1 is reading from the nearest end of the object rather than the zero mark; a quick demonstration of misaligned measurement and its inflated result fixes this for most students. In Q2, students often under-estimate the fingernail as less than 1 cm — let them measure first and then revisit their estimate rather than correcting beforehand, so the surprise does the teaching. For Q3, any small identical toy cars or bottle caps work; if unavailable, rolling three pencils of different lengths serves the same purpose.
materials: Three small toy cars or bottle caps
A thin book to make a ramp

periods.activity_title: Treasure Hunts, Broken Scales, and Number Lines

tasks_in_class.description: Find the longest and shortest route in a treasure-hunt map (walking on yellow 1 cm tiles); find the length of your route in centimetres.
Help Ashwin measure using a broken scale (starting from a non-zero mark); find the two indicated lengths in cm.
Fill the blanks on a number line marked in 10 cm intervals (0–100 cm) and in metres (0–1 m); include 25 cm and 33 m.
A board is 2 m long; a decorative sticker is 20 cm long. How many stickers cover the board completely?

homework.description: Trace your hand on paper; measure its length using a scale.
Use your hand to estimate the measurement of objects; convert into centimetres; verify using a scale. Fill the table.

time_bands.activity: Students open to p.87 and work individually on Let Us Do Q4 (p.87) ("find the longest and shortest route in a treasure-hunt map walking on yellow 1 cm tiles; find the length of your route in centimetres"). They trace each route and count tiles, recording totals before comparing routes.

Teacher displays a broken scale (or draws one on the board starting from 3 cm). Students tackle Let Us Do Q7 (p.88) ("help Ashwin measure using a broken scale starting from a non-zero mark; find the two indicated lengths in cm"), reasoning that the length equals the right-end reading minus the left-end reading.

Students fill Let Us Do Q8 (p.89) ("fill the blanks on a number line marked in 10 cm intervals…"). The class then solves Let Us Do Q9 (p.89) ("a board is 2 m long; a decorative sticker is 20 cm long — how many stickers cover the board?") by first converting 2 m to 200 cm, then dividing.
Pairs share their answers to Q9 and explain the conversion step. Teacher asks: 'What would happen if you forgot to convert?' to consolidate the necessity of working in the same unit before dividing.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q4, students sometimes count corners of tiles twice when tracing a route — demonstrate tracing slowly and counting one tile at a time. The broken scale in Q7 is a high-leverage task; the key error is reading the right-end number as the length rather than subtracting the start mark. For homework, students trace their hand on paper (Let Us Do Q5, p.88) and measure its length with a ruler, then use the hand-span to estimate household objects and verify (Let Us Do Q6, p.88).

periods.activity_title: Wells and Heights — Converting Between Metres and Centimetres

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks so well depths are equal: 2 m = 200 cm; __ m = 400 cm; 6 m = __ cm; __ m = 800 cm.
Match wells with the same depth: four pairs of mixed-unit and pure-cm representations.
Measure each student's height using a measuring tape; complete a class table with height in cm and in m.
Answer questions: tallest height, shortest height, number of children more than 1 m tall, number shorter than 1 m.

time_bands.activity: Students work through Let Us Do Q1a (p.90) ("fill blanks so well depths are equal: 2 m = 200 cm; __ m = 400 cm…"). They use the relationship 1 m = 100 cm established when comparing the metre rope with the measuring tape, multiplying or dividing as needed.

Pairs complete Let Us Do Q1b (p.90) ("match wells with the same depth: four pairs of mixed-unit and pure-cm representations"). Students convert each mixed-unit expression to pure cm before drawing the matching lines.

Class activity from Let Us Explore (p.90) ("measure each student's height using a measuring tape; complete a class table with height in cm and in m"). Students take turns being measured while a partner reads the tape; each child records their height in both forms in the table.

Students answer Let Us Explore Q1–Q4 (p.91) ("tallest height, shortest height, number more than 1 m tall, number shorter than 1 m") using the completed class table, practising the comparison of mixed and pure-cm representations.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently write, for example, 1 m 20 cm as 120 m rather than 120 cm — spending a moment writing the two representations side by side on the board (120 cm = 1 m 20 cm) before Q1a prevents this. In the height activity, students sometimes read the tape from the wrong end; ensure the tape is held with zero at the floor and the reader looks horizontally at the top of the head. Having a spare tape or metre rope helps keep the activity moving without long queues.
materials: Class height recording chart or whiteboard grid

tasks_in_class.description: Colour the bricks on Bhola's garden boundary; count how many bricks are needed to make the boundary.
Bhola made boundaries in three ways; circle the boundary that is longest.
Find perimeter of shapes on dot grid (1 cm spacing); colour longest boundary blue, shortest green; tick shapes with the same length.

time_bands.activity: Students open to p.91 and work on Let Us Do (Bhola's garden) ("colour the bricks on Bhola's garden boundary; count how many bricks are needed to make the boundary"). They trace the outer edge carefully and count each brick unit, writing the total.

Students examine the three boundary options in Let Us Do Q1 (p.92) ("Bhola made boundaries in three ways; circle the boundary that is longest"). Pairs discuss how they are comparing — by counting brick lengths — before circling their answer.

Students work through Let Us Do Q2 (a–c) (p.92) ("find perimeter of shapes on dot grid 1 cm spacing; colour longest boundary blue, shortest green; tick shapes with the same length"). They count side lengths around each shape on the 1 cm dot grid, add them, and compare totals.

periods.teacher_notes: The idea that perimeter means going all the way around the outside is new; a common error is counting only three sides of a four-sided figure. Walking a finger around the shape on the dot grid before counting helps students avoid this. In Q2, students sometimes count the dots rather than the spaces between dots — a quick demonstration with two dots ('one space = one centimetre') clarifies this before independent work.

tasks_in_class.description: Do any of the six shapes (A–F) have the same perimeter? Tick them.
Tick the garden with the minimum perimeter from four options.
Draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm on a 1 cm dot grid.

time_bands.activity: Students measure all six shapes A–F in Let Us Do Q3 (p.93) ("do any of the six shapes have the same perimeter? tick them"), recording each perimeter before comparing. Teacher asks: 'Can two shapes look very different but have the same perimeter?' after students share results.

Students work on Let Us Do Q4 (p.93) ("tick the garden with the minimum perimeter from four options"). They calculate each garden's perimeter on the dot grid and identify the smallest value, explaining why a smaller perimeter means less fencing.

Students tackle Let Us Do Q6 (p.94) ("draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm on a 1 cm dot grid"). They plan their shapes by choosing side lengths that sum to 20, draw them on the dot grid, then verify by counting the boundary.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q3, students are often surprised that shapes of different appearance share the same perimeter — this is the key insight of the task, so let the surprise land before explaining. A frequent error in Q6 is drawing an open figure; remind students to close every shape by returning to the starting dot. Having students count their perimeter aloud after drawing catches this error before they finish.

periods.activity_title: Measuring Real Boundaries in the Classroom

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate then measure the perimeters of desk, blackboard, classroom floor, and two chosen objects; record estimated and actual values in cm/m.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the task from Let Us Do Q5 (p.94) ("estimate then measure the perimeters of desk, blackboard, classroom floor, and two chosen objects; record estimated and actual values in cm/m"). Each student first fills the estimate column for all objects before any measuring begins.

Groups of three rotate around the designated objects — desk, blackboard, and two objects of their choice — measuring each perimeter with a metre rope or measuring tape and recording actual values in the table. The classroom floor perimeter is measured as a class with one group leading.

Whole-class discussion: which estimates were closest? Students compare their estimated and actual values and note whether their estimates improved across the five objects. Teacher consolidates the lesson by asking students to state what perimeter means in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students measuring the classroom floor often measure only one length and one breadth rather than adding all four sides; prompt them to think of the boundary as a continuous path around the entire floor. For objects with curved edges (e.g. a clock), redirect students to rectangular objects only, since the dot-grid method does not yet extend to curves. Encouraging students to articulate why the perimeter of a large object must be expressed in metres rather than centimetres consolidates the unit-selection skill built throughout the chapter.

items.prompt: Riya has a 1 m rope and a half-metre rope. She wants to find out how far she can hop in one go. She hops and then lays the ropes end to end along the hop. The 1 m rope fits once and the half-metre rope fits once more. How far did Riya hop? Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Riya hopped 1 m and a half, which is 1 and a half metres or 1½ m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Lay the 1 m rope and the ½ m rope end to end and read the total as 1 m + ½ m = 1½ m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically place rope cut-outs end to end; stretch: ask what combination would be needed if she hopped 2 and a quarter metres.

exercise.description: Long jump competition: estimate then measure each student's jump distance using rope combinations; fill the table.

items.prompt: A tailor's measuring tape and a metre rope are both 1 metre long. What can the measuring tape do that the metre rope alone cannot?

options.label: A
options.text: Measure lengths longer than 1 metre

options.label: B
options.text: Show the exact number of centimetres in a length

options.label: C
options.text: Measure weight instead of length

options.label: D
options.text: Tell you the temperature of an object

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The measuring tape shows the exact number of centimetres because it is graduated with marks for every centimetre; the plain rope has no such marks.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The tape carries centimetre marks along its length; a plain rope does not, so it cannot give a centimetre reading.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the length of the tool with its range; both objects are 1 m, so neither measures longer lengths than the other.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses measurement attributes; tapes measure length, not weight.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses measurement tools; temperature requires a thermometer, not a tape.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: hold the tape beside an unmarked string and ask the student to point to where 5 cm would be on each; stretch: ask how many centimetre marks fit on the full 1 m tape and why.

exercise.description: Compare the metre rope with a tailor's measuring tape; observe the marks and discuss how they help measure clearly.

items.prompt: Three children rolled a ball along the floor. The ball rolled 18 cm, 25 cm, and 11 cm. Write the names of the children in order from the shortest roll to the longest roll: Anaya (18 cm), Brij (25 cm), Chetan (11 cm).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Chetan (11 cm), Anaya (18 cm), Brij (25 cm) — shortest to longest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the centimetre values: 11 is least, then 18, then 25.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark the three distances on a number line and ask which mark comes first; stretch: ask by how many centimetres Brij's roll was longer than Chetan's.

exercise.description: Race three toy cars down a ramp; measure the distance each travels in cm and rank them.

items.prompt: During a class activity, four students measured their heights. The heights in centimetres were: 118 cm, 105 cm, 132 cm, and 97 cm. Write each height again using metres and centimetres (for example, 120 cm = 1 m 20 cm).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 118 cm = 1 m 18 cm; 105 cm = 1 m 5 cm; 132 cm = 1 m 32 cm; 97 cm = 0 m 97 cm (or simply 97 cm, less than 1 m).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each value by 100 to find whole metres; the remainder is the centimetres.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a number line from 0 to 200 cm with 1 m marked and ask them to place each height; stretch: ask which two heights together make more than 2 m 30 cm.

exercise.description: Measure each student's height using a measuring tape; complete a class table with height in cm and in m.

items.prompt: You want to measure the perimeter of your maths textbook. What tool would you use and what steps would you follow? Write two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Use a ruler or measuring tape. Measure each of the four sides in centimetres, then add all four measurements together to get the total perimeter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Measure all four sides individually and add the lengths to find the total boundary.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first trace a finger around the book's edge and count how many sides they cross; stretch: ask how the steps would change if the book were not a rectangle.

exercise.description: Estimate then measure the perimeters of desk, blackboard, classroom floor, and two chosen objects; record estimated and actual values in cm/m.

items.prompt: The width of a classroom door is being measured. Which of the following statements is most likely correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The door's width is more than a metre

options.label: B
options.text: The door's width is less than a metre

options.label: C
options.text: The door's width cannot be measured in metres

options.label: D
options.text: The door's width is exactly one centimetre

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The door's width is more than a metre; a standard classroom door is typically wider than 1 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the door's width against the body-scale benchmark of 1 m — a door must be wide enough to walk through, which is more than 1 m.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student lacks body-scale sense of 1 m; the door must accommodate a person walking through, which requires more than 1 m.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the attribute with unit suitability; a door's width is a length and can be measured in metres.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses the metre and centimetre scales wildly; 1 cm is about the width of a fingernail, far too small for a door.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to stretch both arms wide and estimate whether that span is about 1 m, then compare to the door; stretch: ask them to estimate the door height in metres and explain their reasoning.

exercise.description: Recall Grade 3 learning; check and fill blanks — are the given classroom length statements correct or incorrect?

items.section_title: Estimating Lengths of Animals and Objects
items.prompt: A blue whale is 30 m long. A cricket bat is 1 m long. How many cricket bats placed end to end would equal the length of the blue whale? Show how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 30 cricket bats; because 1 bat = 1 m, so 30 bats = 30 m = the whale's length.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Since 1 bat = 1 m, divide the whale's length (30 m) by 1 m to get 30 bats.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 30 cm line on paper and ask the student to mark off 1 cm segments to count; stretch: ask how many bats would equal two blue whales placed end to end.

exercise.description: Answer 5 questions: bus length, bats per whale, buses per two whales, stacked ostriches, crocodiles per whale — using pictured reference lengths.

items.prompt: Meena looks at a grain of rice and says, 'I think this is more than 1 cm long.' She then measures it with a ruler and finds it is less than 1 cm. What does this tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: Meena's ruler is broken

options.label: B
options.text: Her estimate was more than the actual length

options.label: C
options.text: A grain of rice cannot be measured in centimetres

options.label: D
options.text: The grain grew larger after she looked at it

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Her estimate was more than the actual length — she guessed more than 1 cm but the measurement showed less than 1 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the estimated value (more than 1 cm) with the measured value (less than 1 cm); the estimate is larger, so it was an over-estimate.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses an estimation error with a measurement tool error; the ruler is not implicated here.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student believes very small objects cannot be measured in centimetres; centimetres are specifically useful for small objects.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student introduces a fanciful physical explanation instead of reasoning about estimate vs. actual value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student a 1 cm line drawn on paper and ask them to compare a grain of rice to it directly; stretch: ask them to name two objects they think are shorter than 1 cm and explain why.

exercise.description: Estimate lengths (fingernail, eraser, ant, grain, rajma): equal to, more than, or less than 1 cm; verify by measuring. Write things shorter than 1 cm.

items.prompt: A well is 3 m 50 cm deep. Another well is 380 cm deep. Which well is deeper? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The second well (380 cm) is deeper. Convert the first: 3 m 50 cm = 350 cm. Since 380 cm is greater than 350 cm, the second well is deeper.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 3 m 50 cm to 350 cm using 1 m = 100 cm, then compare 350 cm and 380 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a vertical number line with 0 at the top and ask the student to mark both depths; stretch: ask by how many centimetres the deeper well exceeds the shallower one.

exercise.description: Match wells with the same depth: four pairs of mixed-unit and pure-cm representations.

items.prompt: Shape X has sides of 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm, and 5 cm. Shape Y has sides of 7 cm, 3 cm, 7 cm, and 3 cm. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Shape X has a larger perimeter than Shape Y

options.label: B
options.text: Shape Y has a larger perimeter than Shape X

options.label: C
options.text: Both shapes have the same perimeter

options.label: D
options.text: Shape X has no perimeter because all its sides are equal

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both shapes have the same perimeter of 20 cm. Shape X: 5+5+5+5 = 20 cm. Shape Y: 7+3+7+3 = 20 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all four sides of each shape: both sums equal 20 cm.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student focuses on the individual side length (5 is less than 7) rather than the total of all sides.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student focuses on the largest side length (7 > 5) without adding all sides.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses a property of equal sides (a square) with the concept of perimeter; all closed shapes have a perimeter.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to add the sides of each shape step by step and write each running total; stretch: ask the student to draw a third shape with sides of different lengths that also has a perimeter of 20 cm.

exercise.description: Do any of the six shapes (A–F) have the same perimeter? Tick them.

items.prompt: A farmer wants to put a fence around a small plot of land. She has four choices of shape, all drawn on a 1 cm dot grid. Which shape uses the least fencing?

options.label: A
options.text: Shape P

options.label: B
options.text: Shape Q

options.label: C
options.text: Shape R

options.label: D
options.text: Shape S

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape S, with a perimeter of 14 cm, uses the least fencing. P = 16 cm, Q = 16 cm, R = 16 cm, S = 14 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all four sides of each shape and compare: P = 16, Q = 16, R = 16, S = 14; the smallest sum is S.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have selected the shape with equal sides, mistaking visual regularity for small perimeter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have selected the shape with the longest single side, confusing one side with total perimeter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have added only two sides (3+5=8) rather than all four, stopping early.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to add only two opposite sides first for each shape, then double; stretch: ask by how many centimetres Shape S's perimeter is less than Shape P's.

exercise.description: Tick the garden with the minimum perimeter from four options.

items.prompt:
Use your ruler. Measure the three lines below and write their lengths in centimetres. Then write the names of the lines in order from shortest to longest.
Line A: _____________ (draw 4 cm)
Line B: _____________ (draw 7 cm)
Line C: _____________ (draw 2 cm)
items.visual_stimulus: number_line: Line A (4 cm) | Line B (7 cm) | Line C (2 cm)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Line A = 4 cm, Line B = 7 cm, Line C = 2 cm. Order from shortest to longest: Line C, Line A, Line B.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align the zero mark of the ruler with one end of each line and read the centimetre value at the other end; then rank the three values.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student how to align the ruler's zero and make a dot at each end of the line before reading; stretch: ask the student to draw a new line that is exactly 3 cm longer than Line B.

exercise.description: Measure each drawn object using a scale; write the names in increasing order of length.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly fills the blank? 5 m = ___ cm

options.label: A
options.text: 5 cm

options.label: B
options.text: 50 cm

options.label: C
options.text: 500 cm

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 500 cm; because 1 m = 100 cm, so 5 m = 5 × 100 = 500 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of metres by 100: 5 × 100 = 500 cm.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not applied the conversion at all, writing the same number with a different unit label.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has multiplied by 10 instead of 100, confusing dm (decimetres) with cm.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has multiplied by 1000 instead of 100, confusing the metre-to-millimetre conversion with metre-to-centimetre.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count 100 on a number line five times and record the running total; stretch: ask them to convert 5 m 30 cm to pure centimetres.

exercise.description: Fill blanks so well depths are equal: 2 m = 200 cm; __ m = 400 cm; 6 m = __ cm; __ m = 800 cm.

items.prompt: On a 1 cm dot grid, a rectangle has a length of 6 cm and a width of 3 cm. What is the perimeter of the rectangle in centimetres?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the rectangle on dot paper and count each side one at a time; stretch: ask the student to find another rectangle with a different length and width that also has a perimeter of 18 cm.

exercise.description: Find perimeter of shapes on dot grid (1 cm spacing); colour longest boundary blue, shortest green; tick shapes with the same length.

items.prompt: A path on a map is made of square tiles that are each 1 cm long. Route 1 passes through 14 tiles. Route 2 passes through 9 tiles. How many centimetres longer is Route 1 than Route 2?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 cm longer. Route 1 = 14 cm, Route 2 = 9 cm; 14 − 9 = 5 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count tiles to get each route's length in cm, then subtract the shorter from the longer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 0 to 15 and ask the student to mark both route lengths before subtracting; stretch: ask what the total length of both routes combined would be in centimetres.

exercise.description: Find the longest and shortest route in a treasure-hunt map (walking on yellow 1 cm tiles); find the length of your route in centimetres.

items.prompt: Kavya places her ruler with its zero mark missing. The left end of a ribbon lines up at the 4 cm mark and the right end lines up at the 11 cm mark on the ruler. How long is the ribbon in centimetres?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the start reading from the end reading: 11 − 4 = 7 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to mark 4 and 11 on a number line and count the gaps between them; stretch: ask what the reading at the right end would be if the same ribbon started at the 6 cm mark instead.

exercise.description: Help Ashwin measure using a broken scale (starting from a non-zero mark); find the two indicated lengths in cm.

items.prompt: A shelf is 3 m long. Each book placed on it is 30 cm wide. How many books can fit on the shelf side by side?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 10 books. Convert: 3 m = 300 cm. Number of books = 300 ÷ 30 = 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 3 m to 300 cm using 1 m = 100 cm, then divide 300 by 30.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 300 cm line and ask the student to mark off 30 cm segments and count them; stretch: ask how many books would fit if each book were 25 cm wide instead.

exercise.description: A board is 2 m long; a decorative sticker is 20 cm long. How many stickers cover the board completely?

items.prompt: Draw two different shapes on a 1 cm dot grid, each with a perimeter of 12 cm. Label each shape and write the length of every side.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two closed shapes on the dot grid whose sides sum to 12 cm are correct. Examples: a rectangle with sides 4 cm, 2 cm, 4 cm, 2 cm (4+2+4+2 = 12); a rectangle with sides 5 cm, 1 cm, 5 cm, 1 cm (5+1+5+1 = 12); an L-shape or other polygon whose boundary totals 12 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose side lengths that add to 12, draw the closed shape on dot paper, and verify by counting the boundary.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: suggest starting with a square and ask what side length would give a perimeter of 12 cm; stretch: draw a third shape with a perimeter of 12 cm that is not a rectangle.

exercise.description: Draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm on a 1 cm dot grid.
